lessons.title: Why Split the Power Three Ways?
lessons.title_zh: 權力為什麼要分成三份？
lessons.level: 高中以上 · High school and up
lessons.blurb_en: Pass a bill, veto it, override the veto: choose a move in a 3D model of Washington and watch an arrow fly from the branch that acts to the branch it checks. Read Montesquieu and Federalist No. 47 in the original, then work out what happens to a bill after a veto.
lessons.blurb_zh: 通過法案、否決、推翻否決——在華盛頓的 3D 模型裡選一招，看箭頭從出手的部門飛向被牽制的部門。讀孟德斯鳩與《聯邦論》第四十七篇的原文，再算算一項法案被否決之後還有幾條路。
lessons.big_idea_en: The Constitution divides the work of government among three branches so that no single person or group holds all of it. Then it gives each branch a limited share in the work of the others, so that each can slow or stop the other two. The first idea is called the separation of powers. The second is called checks and balances.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 憲法把政府的工作分給三個部門，讓任何一個人或一群人都拿不到全部的權力；接著又讓每個部門在別的部門的工作裡各有一小份，於是每一個都能拖慢或擋下另外兩個。前一個想法叫權力分立，後一個叫制衡。

lab.title_en: Three Branches, Each Able to Stop the Others
lab.title_zh: 三個部門，誰都擋得住誰
lab.how_en: The three buildings stand for Congress, the President, and the courts. Choose a move from the buttons below. An arrow flies from the branch that acts to the branch it checks, and the panel shows what the move is, where the Constitution provides for it, and an example from history. Many panels end with a question: what can the other side do? Press the answer and the exchange goes on. The grid keeps track of which of the six directions you have seen.
lab.how_zh: 三棟建築代表國會、總統和法院。從下面的按鈕選一招：箭頭會從出手的部門飛向被牽制的部門，右邊欄說明這一招是什麼、憲法在哪裡規定，以及歷史上的一個例子。很多說明欄最後會問：對方可以怎麼回應？按下答案，這場往來就接著演下去。右下角的方格記著六個方向裡你看過哪幾個。
lab.scale_en: A simplified diagram, not to scale; the positions of the buildings and the directions they face are simplified too. The arrows show who acts on whom. They do not show how often each move is used: some are everyday events, and some have happened only a handful of times.
lab.scale_zh: 這是簡化的示意圖，不照比例；三棟建築的位置與朝向也簡化過。箭頭表示誰對誰出手，不代表這一招有多常用——有的天天發生，有的在歷史上只出現過幾次。

actions.text_en: A bill must pass both the House and the Senate in the same form, which is already a check inside Congress. It is then presented to the President. This is an ordinary step, not a check on another branch, but it is where most exchanges begin.
actions.text_zh: 法案必須以相同的內容在眾議院和參議院都通過——這已經是國會內部的一道牽制。接著法案送交總統。這是平常的步驟，不算牽制別的部門，但大多數的往來從這裡開始。
actions.quote: Every Bill which shall have passed the House of Representatives and the Senate, shall, before it become a Law, be presented to the President of the United States;

actions.text_en: If two thirds of the House and then two thirds of the Senate vote for the bill again, it becomes law without the President's signature.
actions.text_zh: 如果眾議院三分之二、接著參議院三分之二再次表決通過，法案不必總統簽署就成為法律。
actions.quote: If after such Reconsideration two thirds of that House shall agree to pass the Bill, it shall be sent, together with the Objections, to the other House, by which it shall likewise be reconsidered, and if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a Law.
actions.eg_en: Congress first overrode a veto on March 3, 1845, more than half a century after the first veto. It has done so 112 times in all (Senate records, read in October 2026).
actions.eg_zh: 國會第一次推翻否決是在 1845 年 3 月 3 日，距離第一次否決已經超過半個世紀。到現在一共推翻過 112 次（參議院紀錄，2026 年 10 月查閱）。

actions.en: Congress decides what money may be spent
actions.zh: 國會決定錢可以怎麼花
actions.text_en: The executive branch runs the departments and the armed forces, but it may spend only what Congress has approved by law. This is often called the power of the purse.
actions.text_zh: 行政部門管理各部會和軍隊，但只能花國會以法律核准的錢。這常被稱為「錢包的權力」（power of the purse）。
actions.quote: No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law;

actions.text_en: The President's nominees for the courts and for the top executive posts take office only if the Senate consents, and a treaty needs two thirds of the senators present. The Senate can vote no, or simply not act.
actions.text_zh: 總統提名的法官與行政部門高階官員，要參議院同意才能就任；條約則需要出席參議員三分之二同意。參議院可以表決否決，也可以乾脆不處理。
actions.quote: … he shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the supreme Court, and all other Officers of the United States …
actions.eg_en: In December 1795 the Senate voted 10 to 14 against George Washington's choice for chief justice, John Rutledge. It was the first Supreme Court nomination the Senate rejected; there have been twelve such rejections by vote.
actions.eg_zh: 1795 年 12 月，參議院以 10 票對 14 票否決了華盛頓提名的首席大法官人選拉特利奇（John Rutledge）。這是參議院第一次否決最高法院的提名；經表決否決的一共有十二次。

actions.en: Congress impeaches and tries the President
actions.text_en: The House may impeach, which means to bring formal charges. The Senate then holds the trial, with the chief justice presiding when a President is tried, and conviction takes two thirds of the members present. The only penalties are removal from office and a bar on holding office again.
actions.text_zh: 眾議院可以提出彈劾，也就是正式提出指控。接著由參議院審判；受審的是總統時，由首席大法官主持。定罪需要出席議員三分之二同意。處罰只有免職，以及不得再擔任公職。
actions.quote: The President, Vice President and all civil Officers of the United States, shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.
actions.eg_en: In 1868 the vote in the Senate to convict President Andrew Johnson was 35 to 19, one vote short of two thirds, so he was acquitted and stayed in office. No President has ever been removed by conviction.
actions.eg_zh: 1868 年，參議院以 35 票對 19 票表決是否將總統安德魯．詹森定罪——離三分之二只差一票，所以他留任。從來沒有一位總統因為被定罪而去職。

actions.en: Congress impeaches and removes a judge
actions.zh: 國會彈劾法官並將其免職
actions.text_en: Federal judges keep their offices “during good Behaviour,” which in practice means for life. The one way to remove a judge is the same process used for a President: impeachment by the House and conviction by two thirds of the Senate.
actions.text_zh: 聯邦法官「品行端正」即得繼續任職，實際上就是終身職。要把法官免職只有一條路，和對總統用的是同一套程序：眾議院彈劾，參議院三分之二定罪。
actions.quote: The Judges, both of the supreme and inferior Courts, shall hold their Offices during good Behaviour …
actions.eg_en: The Senate has convicted eight officials in impeachment trials since 1789. All eight were federal judges (Senate records, read in October 2026).
actions.eg_zh: 1789 年以來，參議院在彈劾審判中一共將八名官員定罪，八人全是聯邦法官（參議院紀錄，2026 年 10 月查閱）。

actions.en: Congress shapes the courts and can answer a ruling
actions.zh: 國會決定法院的編制，也可以回應判決
actions.text_en: The Constitution creates only the Supreme Court. Congress creates the lower courts and sets the number of justices by law: six in 1789, and nine since 1869. When Congress and the states disagree with a ruling on the Constitution, they can amend the Constitution.
actions.text_zh: 憲法只設立了最高法院。下級法院由國會設立，大法官的人數也由國會以法律決定：1789 年是六位，1869 年以來是九位。國會與各州不同意法院對憲法的某項判決時，可以修憲。
actions.quote: To constitute Tribunals inferior to the supreme Court;
actions.eg_en: In Chisholm v. Georgia (1793) the Supreme Court let a citizen of one state sue another state in federal court. The Eleventh Amendment, ratified in 1795, reversed that result.
actions.eg_zh: 1793 年的 Chisholm v. Georgia 案，最高法院准許一州的公民在聯邦法院控告另一個州。1795 年批准的第十一條修正案推翻了這個結果。

actions.text_en: The President may refuse to sign a bill and send it back to Congress with written objections. The word “veto” is not in the Constitution; the text speaks of returning the bill.
actions.text_zh: 總統可以拒絕簽署，把法案連同書面的異議退回國會。憲法裡沒有 veto 這個字，條文說的是「退回」法案。
actions.quote: If he approve he shall sign it, but if not he shall return it, with his Objections to that House in which it shall have originated, who shall enter the Objections at large on their Journal, and proceed to reconsider it.
actions.eg_en: George Washington issued the first veto on April 5, 1792. Presidents have vetoed 2,599 bills and joint resolutions since then (Senate records, read in October 2026).
actions.eg_zh: 華盛頓在 1792 年 4 月 5 日行使了第一次否決。從那時起，歷任總統一共否決了 2,599 項法案與聯合決議案（參議院紀錄，2026 年 10 月查閱）。

actions.text_en: Judges do not choose their own successors. Every federal judge is nominated by the President, so over time the elected branches decide who sits on the courts. The nomination then needs the Senate's consent.
actions.text_zh: 法官不能自己挑接班人。每一位聯邦法官都由總統提名，所以時間一久，是民選的部門在決定誰坐上法官席。提名之後還要參議院同意。
actions.quote: … he shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint … Judges of the supreme Court …
actions.eg_en: Presidents have sent the Senate 165 nominations for the Supreme Court since 1789 (Senate table, which runs through 2022).
actions.eg_zh: 1789 年以來，歷任總統一共向參議院送出 165 次最高法院的提名（參議院的統計表，列到 2022 年）。

actions.text_en: The President may set aside the punishment for a federal crime, usually after a court has convicted and sentenced the person. The power does not reach impeachment, and it does not reach crimes under state law. It is sometimes described as a check on the courts, although it works case by case.
actions.text_zh: 總統可以免除聯邦罪行的刑罰，通常是在法院定罪、判刑之後。這項權力不及於彈劾案，也不及於州法上的罪行。有人把它看成對法院的一種牽制，不過它是一個案子一個案子行使的。
actions.quote: … he shall have Power to grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offences against the United States, except in Cases of Impeachment.

actions.en: The courts refuse to apply an unconstitutional law
actions.zh: 法院拒絕適用違憲的法律
actions.text_en: When a case turns on a law that conflicts with the Constitution, a court follows the Constitution and treats the law as void. This is judicial review. The Constitution does not provide for it in so many words; the Supreme Court set out the reasoning in 1803.
actions.text_zh: 當一個案子牽涉到牴觸憲法的法律時，法院依據憲法判決，把那項法律當作無效。這就是司法審查。憲法並沒有明文規定這項權力；最高法院在 1803 年說明了它的道理。
actions.quote: It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.
actions.cite: Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall
actions.eg_en: In Marbury v. Madison the Court found that part of the act that had organized the federal courts gave the Court a power the Constitution did not allow, and it declined to use that power.
actions.eg_zh: 在 Marbury v. Madison 案裡，最高法院認定當初設立聯邦法院的那部法律，有一部分給了最高法院憲法所不允許的權力，因此拒絕行使那項權力。

actions.en: The courts rule against an executive order
actions.zh: 法院判定行政命令不合法
actions.text_en: Courts also decide whether the President and the departments have acted within the Constitution and the laws. If they have not, the court can order the action stopped.
actions.text_zh: 法院也判斷總統與各部會的作為有沒有超出憲法與法律的範圍。超出的話，法院可以下令停止。
actions.quote: In the framework of our Constitution, the President's power to see that the laws are faithfully executed refutes the idea that he is to be a lawmaker.
actions.cite: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952), Justice Hugo Black for the Court
actions.eg_en: In 1952 President Harry Truman ordered the Secretary of Commerce to take possession of most of the nation's steel mills. The Supreme Court held that neither a law nor the Constitution gave him that power, and that the order could not stand.
actions.eg_zh: 1952 年，杜魯門總統下令商務部長接管全國大部分的鋼鐵廠。最高法院判定，沒有任何法律、憲法也沒有給他這項權力，這道命令不能成立。

paras: In 1788, while the states were deciding whether to ratify the Constitution, James Madison named the danger it was built to avoid. “The accumulation of all powers legislative, executive and judiciary in the same hands,” he wrote in The Federalist No. 47, “… may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.” The thought was not his own. Forty years earlier the French writer Montesquieu had argued that liberty cannot last where the power to make laws, the power to carry them out, and the power to judge are joined in one person or one body. Madison called him “the oracle who is always consulted and cited on this subject.” The practical question was how to keep those three powers apart.

The first answer was separation. The Constitution gives the legislative power to Congress in Article I, the executive power to a President in Article II, and the judicial power to the courts in Article III. Each branch is chosen in a different way and for a different length of time: representatives for two years, senators for six, a President for four, and federal judges for as long as they show “good Behaviour.” The branches are also kept apart in their membership. No one who holds a federal office may sit in Congress at the same time, so a cabinet secretary cannot also be a senator. In a parliamentary system, by contrast, the ministers who run the government are usually members of the legislature.

Separation alone was not expected to hold. Madison warned in The Federalist No. 48 that “power is of an encroaching nature,” and he doubted that boundaries written into a document, which he called “parchment barriers,” would stop a determined branch. So the Constitution adds a second device. Rather than sealing the branches off from one another, it gives each a limited share in the work of the others. The President takes part in lawmaking through the veto. The Senate takes part in appointments. Congress can remove a President or a judge. This arrangement is called checks and balances. Madison argued that it keeps faith with Montesquieu, whose rule forbids one branch to hold the whole power of another.

Lawmaking shows how the checks work. A bill must pass both the House and the Senate, which is already a check inside Congress. It then goes to the President, who may sign it or return it with objections. That return is the veto, although the word never appears in the Constitution. Congress can still make the bill law if two thirds of each house vote to override. That is hard to do. According to the Senate's records, presidents have vetoed 2,599 bills and joint resolutions since 1789. More than a thousand were pocket vetoes, which cannot be overridden; of the 1,533 others, Congress has overridden 112. The first veto came in 1792, and the first override not until 1845.

Other checks run through appointments and money. The President chooses ambassadors, department heads, and federal judges, but only “by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate,” and a treaty needs the agreement of two thirds of the senators present. The Senate has voted down a nomination to the Supreme Court twelve times, the first of them in 1795. Congress also holds what is often called the power of the purse. In the words of Article I, “No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law.” A President commands the armed forces and directs the departments, but cannot lawfully spend money that Congress has not approved.

The most drastic check is removal. The House of Representatives may impeach, that is, bring formal charges against, the President, other civil officers, and judges for “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.” The Senate then holds a trial, and conviction requires two thirds of the members present. Removal has been rare. As of 2026 the House has impeached officials twenty-two times, and the Senate has convicted eight of them, every one a federal judge. No President has been removed in this way. In 1868 the vote in the Senate to convict President Andrew Johnson was 35 to 19, one vote short of two thirds, so he was acquitted.

The courts hold a check that the Constitution does not spell out. In Marbury v. Madison, decided in 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall wrote: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” The same opinion reasoned that a law contrary to the Constitution is void. This power, called judicial review, lets courts refuse to apply laws and executive actions that violate the Constitution. Yet the courts are checked as well. Judges are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and Congress decides how many justices sit on the Supreme Court. As Alexander Hamilton observed, the judiciary has “neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment”: it depends on the executive branch to carry out its decisions.

All of this has a cost. A system in which every branch can say no tends to be slow, and it can stall when the branches disagree, a condition that news reports call gridlock. Critics since the nineteenth century have argued that dividing power also divides responsibility, so that voters cannot easily tell whom to hold to account. Defenders answer that the delay is deliberate. Justice Louis Brandeis wrote in 1926 that the separation of powers was adopted “not to promote efficiency but to preclude the exercise of arbitrary power.” Whether that trade is worth making is a real argument about how governments should be built, and the Design Debate card in this lesson sets out both sides.
paras_zh: 1788 年，各州還在決定要不要批准憲法的時候，麥迪遜點出了這部憲法想要避開的危險。他在《聯邦論》第四十七篇寫道：「把立法、行政、司法的一切權力集中在同一批人手裡……完全可以說就是暴政的定義。」這個想法不是他發明的。四十年前，法國作家孟德斯鳩（Montesquieu）就主張：制定法律的權力、執行法律的權力和審判的權力，如果合在同一個人或同一個機構手上，自由就保不住。麥迪遜稱他是「談到這個題目，人人都要請教、都要引用的權威」。真正的難題是實際上要怎麼把這三種權力分開。
第一個答案是「分開」。憲法在第一條把立法權交給國會，第二條把行政權交給總統，第三條把司法權交給法院。每個部門產生的方式不同，任期也不同：眾議員兩年、參議員六年、總統四年，聯邦法官則是「品行端正」就一直做下去。三個部門連成員也是分開的：擔任聯邦官職的人不能同時當國會議員，所以內閣部長不可能兼任參議員。相對地，在內閣制（parliamentary system）裡，負責施政的閣員通常就是國會議員。

光是分開，制憲者並不認為撐得住。麥迪遜在《聯邦論》第四十八篇警告：「權力具有侵略的本性」；他也懷疑，寫在文件裡的界線——他稱之為「羊皮紙上的柵欄」（parchment barriers）——擋不擋得住一個鐵了心要擴權的部門。於是憲法加上第二個設計：不是把三個部門彼此封死，而是讓每個部門在別的部門的工作裡各有一小份。總統靠否決參與立法；參議院參與人事任命；國會可以把總統或法官免職。這套安排叫做制衡（checks and balances）。麥迪遜主張，這樣並沒有違背孟德斯鳩的原則——那條原則禁止的，是一個部門握有另一個部門的「全部」權力。

從立法可以看出制衡怎麼運作。法案必須在眾議院和參議院都通過，這已經是國會內部的一道牽制。接著法案送到總統手上，總統可以簽署，也可以附上異議退回。這個「退回」就是否決（veto），雖然憲法裡從頭到尾沒有這個字。國會如果兩院各有三分之二表決推翻（override），法案仍然成為法律——但這很難做到。依參議院的紀錄，1789 年以來歷任總統一共否決了 2,599 項法案與聯合決議案，其中一千多項是不能推翻的「口袋否決」（pocket veto，學術名詞作「袋中否決」）；其餘 1,533 項裡，國會推翻了 112 項。第一次否決在 1792 年，第一次推翻要等到 1845 年。
另外一些牽制走的是人事和錢。大使、各部會首長和聯邦法官由總統挑選，但必須「經參議院的建議與同意」；條約則需要出席參議員三分之二同意。參議院曾經十二次表決否決最高法院的提名，第一次在 1795 年。國會還握有常被稱為「錢包的權力」的那項權力——第一條的原文是：「除依法律所定的撥款外，不得從國庫提取任何款項。」總統統率軍隊、指揮各部會，但不能合法地花國會沒有核准的錢。

最激烈的一道牽制是免職。眾議院可以對總統、其他文職官員和法官提出彈劾（impeach）——也就是正式提出指控——罪名是「叛國、賄賂或其他重罪與輕罪」。接著由參議院審判，定罪需要出席議員三分之二同意。真正被免職的很少。到 2026 年為止，眾議院一共彈劾過二十二次，參議院將其中八人定罪，八人全是聯邦法官。沒有一位總統是這樣去職的。1868 年，參議院表決是否將安德魯．詹森總統定罪，結果是 35 票對 19 票，離三分之二只差一票，所以他沒有被定罪。

法院握有的那道牽制，憲法並沒有明寫。1803 年判決的 Marbury v. Madison 案裡，首席大法官馬歇爾寫道：「說明法律是什麼，斷然是司法部門的職權與責任。」同一份意見書推論：牴觸憲法的法律是無效的。這項權力叫做司法審查（judicial review），法院可以據此拒絕適用違反憲法的法律和行政作為。不過法院自己也受到牽制：法官由總統提名、參議院同意；最高法院有幾位大法官由國會決定。而且正如漢彌爾頓所說，司法部門「既沒有武力，也沒有意志，只有判斷」——它的判決要靠行政部門去執行。

這一切是有代價的。每個部門都能說「不」的制度往往走得很慢，各部門意見不合時還可能停擺——新聞裡把這種狀況叫做僵局（gridlock）。從十九世紀起就有批評者主張：分散權力也就分散了責任，選民不容易看出該找誰負責。辯護的人則回答：慢是刻意的。布蘭戴斯大法官（Louis Brandeis）在 1926 年寫道，採用權力分立「不是為了提高效率，而是為了防止權力被恣意行使」。這筆交換值不值得，是關於政府該怎麼設計的一場真正的爭論；這一課的「制度的爭論」卡會把兩邊都寫出來。
questions: Explain the difference between “separation of powers” and “checks and balances.” Why did Madison think the first would not work without the second?
Choose one check from the reading and trace a complete exchange: who acts first, how the other branch can respond, and what finally decides the outcome.
The reading says that a system in which every branch can say no “has a cost.” What is the cost, and what do defenders of the system say it buys?
answers: Separation of powers means giving the three kinds of power to three different branches with different members. Checks and balances means giving each branch a small part in the others' work, such as the veto or the Senate's consent to appointments, so that it can resist them. Madison thought that written boundaries alone (“parchment barriers”) would not stop a branch from reaching for more power, because “power is of an encroaching nature.” Each branch needed its own means of defense.

Sample answer: Congress passes a bill. The President vetoes it by returning it with objections. Congress can respond by voting again; if two thirds of the House and two thirds of the Senate approve, the bill becomes law anyway. If either house falls short, the veto stands. Other good answers: nomination and Senate consent; impeachment by the House and trial in the Senate; a court ruling answered by a constitutional amendment.

The cost is speed and sometimes action itself: laws are harder to pass, and when the branches disagree the government can reach gridlock. Critics add that it becomes harder for voters to know who is responsible. Defenders say the delay protects liberty, because no one branch can act alone; in Brandeis's words, the purpose was “not to promote efficiency but to preclude the exercise of arbitrary power.”

quiz.q: A cabinet secretary wants to keep her post and also serve as a senator. Why does the Constitution forbid this?
options: Senators must be older than cabinet secretaries
No one holding a federal office may be a member of Congress at the same time, which keeps the branches separate in their membership
The President may not appoint anyone from the Senate's home state
Cabinet secretaries are chosen by the Supreme Court

quiz.q: Madison doubted that “parchment barriers” would be enough. What did he mean?
options: The Constitution was written on material that would not last
Courts would refuse to read the Constitution
Boundaries written in a document will not by themselves stop a branch from taking more power
The states would ignore the federal government

options: It becomes law, because both houses passed it twice

It goes to the Supreme Court to decide
It fails, because the Senate is short of two thirds

options: Courts depend on the executive branch to carry out their decisions
Federal judges serve during good behavior

Marbury v. Madison was decided in 1803

Judges are impeached by the Supreme Court
Impeachment has been used only eight times

parts_head.eyebrow: Try It in the Model · 在模型裡試試

parts.text_en: Three arrows in a row: Congress sends a bill, the President sends it back, and Congress answers with two thirds of each house. Notice that the veto stands unless Congress can gather two thirds in both houses.
parts.text_zh: 連續三道箭頭：國會送出法案，總統把它退回，國會再用兩院各三分之二回應。注意：除非國會能在兩院都湊到三分之二，否則否決就成立。

parts.en: Who puts a judge on the bench?
parts.zh: 誰讓一位法官坐上法官席？
parts.text_en: The President nominates, the Senate may refuse, and Congress decides how many seats there are. The courts are the one branch whose members are chosen entirely by the other two.
parts.text_zh: 總統提名，參議院可以不同意，國會則決定有幾個席位。三個部門裡，只有法院的成員完全由另外兩個部門來決定。

parts.en: The check that is not in the text
parts.zh: 條文裡沒有寫的那道牽制
parts.text_en: Two arrows leave the Supreme Court: one toward Congress, when a law conflicts with the Constitution, and one toward the President, when an order goes beyond his lawful power. Neither is spelled out in Article III.
parts.text_zh: 兩道箭頭從最高法院出發：一道指向國會（法律牴觸憲法時），一道指向總統（命令超出他合法的權限時）。這兩項在第三條裡都沒有明寫。

parts.text_en: The same two-step process, accusation in the House and trial in the Senate, can remove a President or a judge. Compare the two panels: one has never ended in a conviction, and the other has eight times.
parts.text_zh: 同一套兩步驟的程序——眾議院指控、參議院審判——可以把總統免職，也可以把法官免職。比一比這兩個說明欄：一種從來沒有以定罪收場，另一種有八次。

lessons.parts_note_en: When you have watched all four, look at the grid in the panel. Each of the three branches should have checked both of the others: six directions in all.
lessons.parts_note_zh: 四場都看過之後，看看說明欄裡的方格：三個部門應該各自牽制過另外兩個——一共六個方向。

match.lead_en: Ten moves. For each one, choose which branch is acting and which branch is being checked. There is no timer, and you can keep choosing until you find it; the game counts the ones you get on the first try.
match.lead_zh: 十招。每一題選出是哪個部門出手、牽制的是哪個部門。不計時，可以一直選到對為止；遊戲會記下你第一次就答對的題數。

questions.zh: 不簽署法案，附上書面異議退回

questions.why_zh: 這就是否決：總統牽制國會的立法權（第一條第七項）。

questions.zh: 提名一位新的最高法院大法官
questions.why_en: Judges do not pick their successors. By choosing who sits on the courts, the President checks the judiciary (Article II, Section 2).
questions.why_zh: 法官不能自己挑接班人。總統藉由決定誰當法官，來牽制司法部門（第二條第二項）。
questions.hint_en: The question is about who chooses, and whose membership is being chosen.
questions.hint_zh: 重點是「誰來選」，以及被決定成員的是哪個部門。

questions.en: Refusing to approve a treaty the President has signed
questions.zh: 不同意總統簽署的條約
questions.why_en: A treaty needs two thirds of the senators present (Article II, Section 2). The Senate checks the President.
questions.why_zh: 條約需要出席參議員三分之二同意（第二條第二項）。這是參議院牽制總統。
questions.hint_en: The Senate is part of which branch?
questions.hint_zh: 參議院屬於哪一個部門？

questions.en: Impeaching a federal judge and removing him from office
questions.zh: 彈劾一名聯邦法官並將他免職
questions.why_en: The House impeaches and the Senate tries. This has ended in conviction eight times, always of judges.
questions.why_zh: 由眾議院彈劾、參議院審判。這套程序有八次以定罪收場，對象都是法官。
questions.hint_en: Which branch holds impeachment trials?
questions.hint_zh: 彈劾審判是在哪個部門進行的？

questions.en: Ruling that a presidential order goes beyond the President's lawful power
questions.zh: 判定總統的一道命令超出他合法的權限
questions.why_en: Courts review executive action too, as in the steel seizure case of 1952.
questions.why_zh: 法院也審查行政部門的作為，例如 1952 年的接管鋼鐵廠案。
questions.hint_en: Who issued the order, and who is judging it?
questions.hint_zh: 命令是誰下的？是誰在審查它？

questions.en: Pardoning a person convicted in a federal court
questions.zh: 赦免一名被聯邦法院定罪的人
questions.why_en: A pardon sets aside a punishment that a court imposed (Article II, Section 2).
questions.why_zh: 赦免免除的是法院所判的刑罰（第二條第二項）。
questions.hint_en: Whose decision is being set aside?
questions.hint_zh: 被擱到一邊的是誰的決定？

questions.en: Setting the number of justices on the Supreme Court by law
questions.zh: 以法律訂定最高法院大法官的人數
questions.why_en: The Constitution leaves the size of the Court to Congress: six justices in 1789, and nine since 1869.
questions.why_zh: 憲法把最高法院的規模交給國會決定：1789 年六位，1869 年以來九位。
questions.hint_en: Laws are made by which branch?
questions.hint_zh: 法律是哪個部門制定的？

questions.en: Keeping a bill unsigned until Congress has adjourned, so that it never becomes law
questions.zh: 把法案放著不簽，直到國會休會，讓它無法成為法律
questions.why_en: This is the pocket veto, and Congress cannot override it: when an adjournment prevents the bill's return, “it shall not be a Law” (Article I, Section 7).
questions.why_zh: 這是口袋否決，國會無法推翻：國會休會致使法案無從退回時，它「不成為法律」（第一條第七項）。
questions.hint_en: Whose bill is it, and who is holding it?
questions.hint_zh: 這是誰的法案？又是誰把它壓著？

match.end_en: Every branch appeared as the one acting and as the one being checked. That is the design: no branch is only a watcher, and none is only watched.
match.end_zh: 每個部門都當過出手的一方，也都當過被牽制的一方。這就是這套設計：沒有哪個部門只管看著別人，也沒有哪個部門只被別人看著。

veto.lead_en: A bill has reached the President's desk. Set how Congress voted, choose what the President does, and read the result. Then change one thing at a time. Try to find the two ways a bill can become law without the President's signature, and the one kind of veto that Congress cannot override.
veto.lead_zh: 一項法案送到了總統桌上。先設定國會怎麼投票，再選總統怎麼做，看看結果；然後一次只改一樣。試著找出法案不經總統簽署也能成為法律的兩種情形，以及國會無法推翻的那一種否決。
veto.marks_en: Each slider has two marks: a majority (218 and 51), which passes a bill, and two thirds (290 and 67), which overrides a veto.
veto.marks_zh: 每支滑桿上有兩個記號：過半數（218 與 51）可以通過法案，三分之二（290 與 67）可以推翻否決。

acts.en: Veto it: return it to Congress with objections
acts.zh: 否決：附上異議退回國會

acts.en: Do nothing for ten days (Sundays not counted)
acts.zh: 十天內不簽也不退回（星期日不算）

veto.adjourn_en: Congress has adjourned during those ten days, so the bill cannot be returned
veto.adjourn_zh: 這十天當中國會已經休會，法案無從退回

fail_congress.en: The bill never reached the President: it needs a majority in both houses first.
fail_congress.zh: 法案根本沒有送到總統手上：它得先在兩院都過半數。

signed.en: Both houses passed it and the President signed it. This is the ordinary route.
signed.zh: 兩院通過、總統簽署。這是最平常的路。

unsigned_law.en: The President neither signed nor returned it, and Congress was still in session, so after ten days it became law “in like Manner as if he had signed it.”
unsigned_law.zh: 總統既沒有簽署也沒有退回，而國會還在開會，所以十天之後它「如同總統已簽署一樣」成為法律。

pocket.en: This is a pocket veto. Because Congress adjourned, the President could not return the bill, and the Constitution says that in that case “it shall not be a Law.” There is nothing for Congress to override, however many votes it has. (Which adjournments count has been disputed between presidents and Congress.)
pocket.zh: 這是口袋否決（pocket veto）。因為國會休會，總統無從退回法案；憲法規定在這種情形下它「不成為法律」。國會不管有多少票，都沒有東西可以推翻。（哪一種休會才算數，總統和國會之間有過爭執。）

overridden.en: The President vetoed it, and two thirds of each house passed it again. The veto is overridden.
overridden.zh: 總統否決了，但兩院各有三分之二再次通過——否決被推翻。

sustained.en: The President vetoed it, and Congress could not gather two thirds in both houses. The veto stands.
sustained.zh: 總統否決了，而國會沒能在兩院都湊到三分之二——否決成立。

veto.bodies_note_en: Counts for 2026: 435 voting seats in the House and 100 in the Senate. The Constitution sets fractions, not head counts, and the two thirds is of the members who vote, so these numbers assume that every seat is filled and every member votes. The tool also assumes that each member votes the same way on the override as on the bill.
veto.bodies_note_zh: 2026 年的數字：眾議院 435 個有表決權的席位、參議院 100 席。憲法寫的是分數而不是人數，而且三分之二是以實際投票的議員來算，所以這裡的票數是假設「席位全部有人、全員投票」。這個小工具還假設：表決推翻否決時，每位議員投的票和當初表決法案時一樣。

items.en: of them pocket vetoes, which cannot be overridden
items.zh: 其中是口袋否決（袋中否決；無法推翻）

record.note_en: Of the 1,533 vetoes that Congress could have tried to override, it overrode 112, about 7 in every 100. The counts include joint resolutions as well as bills. The Senate's table has no “as of” date; these figures were read in October 2026.
record.note_zh: 國會可以嘗試推翻的 1,533 次否決裡，被推翻的有 112 次，大約每 100 次有 7 次。這些數字除了法案，也包括聯合決議案。參議院的表格沒有標示統計截止日；這些數字是 2026 年 10 月查閱的。

clause.eyebrow: What Does the Text Say? · 條文怎麼寫？
clause.en: Three clauses this lesson rests on
clause.zh: 這一課依據的三段條文
clause.lead_en: The words are copied from the National Archives transcription of the Constitution, with the capital letters and spelling of 1787. The first clause keeps the branches apart; the other two let one branch into the work of another.
clause.lead_zh: 原文照美國國家檔案館的憲法謄本逐字抄錄，保留 1787 年的大寫與拼法。第一段把部門分開；另外兩段讓一個部門伸手進另一個部門的工作。

items.cite_zh: 第一條第六項第二款（後半）
items.text: … and no Person holding any Office under the United States, shall be a Member of either House during his Continuance in Office.
items.zh: ……凡在合眾國政府擔任任何官職的人，在其任職期間，不得為國會任何一院的議員。
items.note_en: This is separation in its plainest form: the same person cannot be in two branches at once. It is one of the clearest differences between the presidential system of the United States and a parliamentary system such as Britain's, where ministers normally sit in the legislature.
items.note_zh: 這是最直白的「分開」：同一個人不能同時待在兩個部門。美國的總統制和英國那樣的內閣制，最清楚的差別之一就在這裡——在英國，閣員通常同時是國會議員。

items.cite_en: Article I, Section 7, Clause 2 (the veto and the override)
items.cite_zh: 第一條第七項第二款（否決與推翻否決）
items.text: Every Bill which shall have passed the House of Representatives and the Senate, shall, before it become a Law, be presented to the President of the United States; If he approve he shall sign it, but if not he shall return it, with his Objections to that House in which it shall have originated, who shall enter the Objections at large on their Journal, and proceed to reconsider it. If after such Reconsideration two thirds of that House shall agree to pass the Bill, it shall be sent, together with the Objections, to the other House, by which it shall likewise be reconsidered, and if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a Law.
items.zh: 凡經眾議院與參議院通過的法案，在成為法律之前，應送交合眾國總統。總統如果同意，應予簽署；如果不同意，應附上異議，退回提出該法案的那一院；該院應把異議詳細載入議事錄，並重新審議。重新審議後，如果該院有三分之二同意通過，應將法案連同異議送交另一院，由另一院同樣重新審議；如果也經該院三分之二同意，該法案即成為法律。
items.note_en: The clause continues: a bill not returned within ten days, Sundays excepted, becomes law as if signed, “unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law.” That last phrase is the source of the pocket veto.
items.note_zh: 條文接著規定：法案在十天內（星期日不算）沒有被退回，就如同已簽署一樣成為法律，「除非國會休會致使法案無從退回，在這種情形下它不成為法律」。最後這一句，就是口袋否決的來源。

items.cite_en: Article II, Section 2, Clause 2 (advice and consent)
items.cite_zh: 第二條第二項第二款（參議院的建議與同意）
items.text: He shall have Power, by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, to make Treaties, provided two thirds of the Senators present concur; and he shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate, shall appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, Judges of the supreme Court, and all other Officers of the United States, whose Appointments are not herein otherwise provided for, and which shall be established by Law:
items.zh: 總統經參議院的建議與同意，並經出席參議員三分之二贊成，有締結條約之權；總統提名，並經參議院的建議與同意，任命大使、其他公使與領事、最高法院法官，以及本憲法未另行規定任命方式、而依法律設置的合眾國一切其他官員。
items.note_en: Notice the two different thresholds in one sentence. Treaties need two thirds of the senators present. Appointments need the Senate's consent, and the text does not say how large a vote that takes.
items.note_zh: 注意同一句話裡有兩種不同的門檻：條約要出席參議員的三分之二；人事任命要參議院同意，但條文沒有說需要多少票。

primary.en: Montesquieu, and Madison's reading of him
primary.zh: 孟德斯鳩，以及麥迪遜怎麼讀他
primary.lead_en: Two texts forty years apart. The first is the passage that the authors of the Constitution kept coming back to, in the standard English translation of their century. The second is Madison explaining what that passage does and does not require. Read each slowly before you open the translation; the eighteenth-century spellings (“controul,” “every thing”) are in the originals.
primary.lead_zh: 兩段相隔四十年的文字。第一段是制憲者一再回頭去談的那一段，用的是十八世紀通行的英譯本；第二段是麥迪遜在解釋這段話要求什麼、不要求什麼。先慢慢讀一遍，再打開中譯；十八世紀的拼法（controul、every thing）是原文就有的。

docs.title_en: The Spirit of Laws, Book XI, Chapter 6 (excerpt)
docs.title_zh: 《論法的精神》第十一卷第六章（節錄）
docs.by_en: Charles de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu. First published in French in 1748; English translation by Thomas Nugent, first published in the early 1750s.
docs.by_zh: 孟德斯鳩（Montesquieu）著，1748 年以法文出版；英譯者為 Thomas Nugent，英譯本在 1750 年代初出版。
text: When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty; because apprehensions may arise, lest the same monarch or senate should enact tyrannical laws, to execute them in a tyrannical manner.

Again, there is no liberty, if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers. Were it joined with the legislative, the life and liberty of the subject would be exposed to arbitrary controul; for the judge would be then the legislator. Were it joined to the executive power, the judge might behave with all the violence of an oppressor.

There would be an end of every thing, were the same man, or the same body whether of the nobles or of the people, to exercise those three powers, that of enacting laws, that of executing the public resolutions, and that of judging the crimes or differences of individuals.
text_zh: 當立法權與行政權集中在同一個人或同一個官員團體手上時，自由就不存在了；因為人們會擔心，同一位君主或同一個元老院會制定暴虐的法律，再用暴虐的方式去執行。
同樣地，如果審判權不和立法權、行政權分開，自由也不存在。如果審判權和立法權合在一起，人民的生命與自由就會受到恣意的支配，因為法官就是立法者。如果審判權和行政權合在一起，法官就可能擁有壓迫者的全部暴力。
如果同一個人，或是同一個機構——不論是貴族的還是人民的——行使這三種權力，也就是制定法律的權力、執行公共決議的權力，以及審判罪行或私人爭訟的權力，那就一切都完了。
docs.note_en: Text of Nugent's translation as printed in the London edition of 1758, transcribed by Wikisource from page scans. Public domain. The Chinese translation is ours.
docs.note_zh: 原文依 Nugent 英譯本 1758 年倫敦版，由 Wikisource 依掃描頁面謄錄；公有領域。中譯為本站所譯。

questions.en: Montesquieu gives a separate reason for each combination of powers. What exactly goes wrong when judging is joined to lawmaking, and what goes wrong when it is joined to executing?
questions.zh: 孟德斯鳩替每一種權力的結合各給了一個理由。審判權和立法權合在一起，到底會出什麼問題？和行政權合在一起，又會出什麼問題？

questions.en: He says the danger exists whether the body that holds all three powers is “of the nobles or of the people.” Why would a body elected by the people still be dangerous?
questions.zh: 他說：握有三種權力的機構不論是「貴族的還是人民的」，危險都在。為什麼一個由人民選出來的機構仍然危險？

questions.en: Notice the word “apprehensions” in the first paragraph. Is liberty lost when tyrannical laws are actually passed, or already when people have reason to fear them? What does that tell you about his idea of liberty?
questions.zh: 注意第一段裡的 apprehensions（擔心）。自由是在暴虐的法律真的通過時才失去，還是在人們有理由害怕時就已經失去了？這透露出他心目中的自由是什麼？

docs.by_en: By James Madison, signed “Publius.” Printed in New York newspapers at the end of January 1788; the editors of Madison's papers date it January 30.
docs.by_zh: 麥迪遜著，署名「普布利烏斯」（Publius）。1788 年 1 月底刊登於紐約的報紙；《麥迪遜文集》的編者把日期定在 1 月 30 日。
text: The accumulation of all powers legislative, executive and judiciary in the same hands, whether of one, a few or many, and whether hereditary, self appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny.

From these facts by which Montesquieu was guided it may clearly be inferred, that in saying, “there can be no liberty where the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or body of magistrates,” or, “if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers,” he did not mean that these departments ought to have no partial agency in, or no control over the acts of each other. His meaning, as his own words import, and still more conclusively as illustrated by the example in his eye, can amount to no more than this, that where the whole power of one department is exercised by the same hands which possess the whole power of another department, the fundamental principles of a free constitution, are subverted.
text_zh: 把立法、行政、司法的一切權力集中在同一批人手裡——不論是一個人、少數人還是多數人，也不論是世襲的、自己任命的還是選舉產生的——完全可以說就是暴政的定義。

從孟德斯鳩所依據的這些事實，可以清楚地推斷：當他說「立法權與行政權集中在同一個人或同一個官員團體時，自由便不存在」，或者「審判權如果不和立法權、行政權分開」的時候，他的意思並不是說這些部門對彼此的作為不應該有部分的參與，或者不應該有任何牽制。他的意思——從他自己的話就看得出來，從他眼前的那個實例看得更加確定——只不過是：當一個部門的全部權力，由握有另一個部門全部權力的同一批人行使時，自由憲政的基本原則就被顛覆了。
docs.note_en: Text as given by Founders Online (National Archives), from The Papers of James Madison. The two paragraphs come from different places in the essay. “The example in his eye” is the British constitution, which Montesquieu was describing. Madison's quotations from Montesquieu differ slightly from Nugent's translation above; the editors suggest he may have been translating from a French edition. Other editions, including the Library of Congress text, punctuate the passage differently, print some words in capitals, and date the essay February 1. Public domain. The Chinese translation is ours.
docs.note_zh: 原文依 Founders Online（美國國家檔案館）收錄的《麥迪遜文集》版本；這兩段出自文章裡不同的地方。「他眼前的那個實例」指的是孟德斯鳩當時所描述的英國憲政。麥迪遜引用孟德斯鳩的字句，和上面 Nugent 的譯文略有出入；編者推測他可能是自己從法文本翻譯的。其他版本（包括國會圖書館的文本）標點不同、有些字用大寫，日期則標為 2 月 1 日。公有領域。中譯為本站所譯。

questions.en: Madison separates two things: a branch having “partial agency” in another's work, and one set of hands holding the “whole power” of two branches. Give one example of each from the Constitution.
questions.zh: 麥迪遜把兩件事分開：一個部門在另一個部門的工作裡有「部分的參與」，以及同一批人握有兩個部門的「全部權力」。請從憲法裡各舉一個例子。

questions.en: Madison is answering critics who said the Constitution mixed the powers too much. After reading Montesquieu's own words above, do you find Madison's reading of him convincing? Why or why not?
questions.zh: 麥迪遜是在回應批評者——他們認為這部憲法把權力混得太多。讀過上面孟德斯鳩自己的話之後，你覺得麥迪遜對他的解讀有沒有說服力？為什麼？

debate.eyebrow: The Design Debate · 制度的爭論
debate.en: Is friction the flaw or the design?
debate.lead_en: Democracies have built their governments in two broad ways. Some, like the United States, keep the executive and the legislature apart and let each check the other. Others join them, in what the English writer Walter Bagehot called in 1867 “the nearly complete fusion” of the two powers: the executive is chosen by the legislature and lasts only while it keeps the legislature's support. Each design is stated here in its strongest form, and the card does not choose between them.
debate.lead_zh: 民主國家搭建政府的方式大致有兩種。一種像美國，把行政和立法分開，讓它們互相牽制；另一種把兩者結合起來——英國作家白芝浩（Walter Bagehot）在 1867 年稱之為兩種權力「幾乎完全的融合」：行政首長由立法機關產生，只有在保住立法機關支持的時候才能繼續執政。這裡把兩種設計各用最強的版本寫出來，不替它們分高下。
debate.question_en: Should the power to make laws and the power to carry them out be kept in separate hands that must agree before the government acts, or joined so that one majority, answerable to the voters, can govern?
debate.question_zh: 制定法律的權力和執行法律的權力，應該放在必須彼此同意才能行動的不同人手上，還是結合起來，讓一個要向選民負責的多數能夠施政？

sides.name_en: Separate the powers and let them check each other

points.en: Concentrated power is the greater danger. A government that needs the agreement of several independent bodies will sometimes fail to act, but it is less likely to act against people's rights, because no one of those bodies can do so alone.
points.zh: 集中的權力才是比較大的危險。要好幾個獨立機構都同意才能行動的政府，有時候會做不成事，但也比較不會侵害人民的權利——因為沒有哪一個機構能單獨辦到。

points.en: Bodies chosen in different ways, at different times, by different electorates must each be persuaded. A law that survives all of them rests on broader agreement than one passed by a single majority, and it is less likely to be reversed after the next election.
points.zh: 用不同方式、在不同時間、由不同選民選出來的機構，必須一個一個被說服。通得過這些關卡的法律，共識比單一多數通過的更廣，下次選舉後也比較不會被翻掉。

points.en: Each branch has both a motive and the means to expose what the others do wrong. Rivalry between institutions does some of the work that would otherwise depend on the virtue of the people in office.
points.zh: 每個部門都有動機、也有手段去揭露別的部門做錯的事。機構之間的競爭，分擔了一部分原本只能指望在位者品德的工作。

sides.voice: The doctrine of the separation of powers was adopted by the convention of 1787 not to promote efficiency but to preclude the exercise of arbitrary power. The purpose was not to avoid friction, but, by means of the inevitable friction incident to the distribution of the governmental powers among three departments, to save the people from autocracy.
sides.voice_cite: Justice Louis Brandeis, dissenting in Myers v. United States, 272 U.S. 52 (1926)
sides.voice_zh: 1787 年的制憲會議採用權力分立的原則，不是為了提高效率，而是為了防止權力被恣意行使。目的不在避免摩擦，而是要藉著把政府權力分配給三個部門所必然產生的摩擦，使人民免於專制。——布蘭戴斯大法官，1926 年（不同意見書）

src.label: Cornell LII: Myers v. United States (1926)
Library of Congress: Federalist No. 51

sides.name_en: Join the powers and make one majority answerable
sides.name_zh: 結合，並且讓一個多數負責

points.en: A government has to be able to govern. When the executive is drawn from the majority in the legislature, the people who promise a program are the same people who can pass it and carry it out, so decisions get made.
points.zh: 政府總得要能施政。當行政首長出自立法機關的多數時，提出政綱的人就是有辦法通過它、執行它的同一批人，事情因此做得了決定。

points.en: Clear power means clear responsibility. If things go badly, voters know whom to remove. Where power is divided, each side can blame the other, and it can be hard to say who should answer for the result.
points.zh: 權力清楚，責任才清楚。事情辦壞了，選民知道該把誰換掉。權力分散的地方，每一邊都可以怪另一邊，很難說清楚該由誰為後果負責。

points.en: A deadlock needs an exit. Officials elected for fixed terms can remain at odds for years. A legislature that can dismiss the executive, or be sent back to the voters in a new election, can end a stalemate in weeks.
points.zh: 僵局需要出口。任期固定的民選官員可以對峙好幾年；而一個可以把行政首長換掉、或者可以被解散重選的立法機關，幾個星期就能結束僵持。

sides.voice: If there be one principle clearer than another, it is this: that in any business, whether of government or of mere merchandising, somebody must be trusted, in order that when things go wrong it may be quite plain who should be punished. … Power and strict accountability for its use are the essential constituents of good government.
sides.voice_cite: Woodrow Wilson, Congressional Government (1885), written when he was a young scholar; some words are in italics in the original
sides.voice_zh: 如果有哪一條原則比別的更清楚，那就是：任何事業，不論是政府還是單純的買賣，總得信任某一個人，這樣事情出錯時，才能清清楚楚知道該罰誰。……權力，加上對如何使用權力的嚴格問責，是良好政府的根本要素。——威爾遜，《國會政體》（1885，當時他還是一位年輕的學者）

src.label: Project Gutenberg: Woodrow Wilson, Congressional Government
Project Gutenberg: Walter Bagehot, The English Constitution

debate.close_en: Both designs exist in stable democracies, and many countries combine features of the two. The disagreement is about which risk to guard against first: a government that can do too much, or one that can do too little. This card does not settle it. Which of the arguments above do you find strongest, and what evidence would change your mind?
debate.close_zh: 這兩種設計都存在於穩定的民主國家，也有許多國家混用兩者的特色。分歧在於先防哪一種風險：一個能做太多事的政府，還是一個做不了事的政府。這張卡不替這個問題下結論。上面的論點裡，你覺得哪幾個最有力？什麼樣的證據會讓你改變想法？

taiwan.eyebrow: Compare with Taiwan · 和台灣比一比
taiwan.lead_en: This card compares designs only. It quotes the Constitution of the Republic of China and its Additional Articles from the official Laws and Regulations Database, and it does not say which arrangement is better.
taiwan.lead_zh: 這張卡只比制度的設計，條文引自全國法規資料庫的《中華民國憲法》與《中華民國憲法增修條文》；不評價哪一種安排比較好。

rows.us_en: Three branches: Congress (Article I), the President (Article II), and the courts (Article III).
rows.us_zh: 三個部門：國會（第一條）、總統（第二條）、法院（第三條）。
rows.tw_en: A President and five Yuan: Executive, Legislative, Judicial, Examination, and Control (Constitution, Articles 53, 62, 77, 83, and 90).
rows.tw_zh: 總統之外設五院：行政院、立法院、司法院、考試院、監察院（憲法第 53、62、77、83、90 條）。

rows.us_en: The President is elected separately for a fixed term of four years and does not depend on the confidence of Congress. No officeholder may sit in Congress.
rows.us_zh: 總統另外選出，任期固定四年，不必得到國會的信任才能繼續任職。官員不得兼任國會議員。
rows.tw_en: The President is directly elected and appoints the president of the Executive Yuan. The Executive Yuan is responsible to the Legislative Yuan, which may pass a vote of no confidence; the President may then dissolve the Legislative Yuan (Additional Articles 2 and 3).
rows.tw_zh: 總統由人民直選，並任命行政院院長。行政院對立法院負責；立法院可以通過不信任案，總統在不信任案通過後得解散立法院（增修條文第 2、3 條）。

rows.us_en: The President returns the bill. Overriding takes two thirds of each house. A bill neither signed nor returned within ten days becomes law if Congress is still in session.
rows.us_zh: 總統把法案退回。推翻需要兩院各三分之二。十天內既沒簽署也沒退回的法案，只要國會還在開會，就成為法律。
rows.tw_en: The Executive Yuan, with the President's approval, asks the Legislative Yuan to reconsider within ten days. The bill is upheld if more than half of all members vote for it. If the Legislative Yuan does not decide in time, the original bill lapses.
rows.tw_zh: 行政院經總統核可，於十日內移請立法院覆議。全體立法委員二分之一以上決議維持原案，行政院院長就應接受。立法院逾期沒有議決，原決議失效。

rows.us_en: The House impeaches; the Senate tries the case and convicts by two thirds of the members present.
rows.us_zh: 眾議院彈劾；參議院審判，出席議員三分之二同意即定罪。
rows.tw_en: The Legislative Yuan impeaches, on the proposal of more than half and the vote of more than two thirds of all its members. The case then goes to the Constitutional Court, and the President is removed if the Court upholds it (Additional Articles 2, 4, and 5).
rows.tw_zh: 立法院提出彈劾案，須經全體立法委員二分之一以上提議、三分之二以上決議；接著聲請司法院大法官審理，經憲法法庭判決成立，被彈劾人即解職（增修條文第 2、4、5 條）。

rows.topic_en: Who decides what the constitution means
rows.us_en: The ordinary federal courts, with the Supreme Court at the top. The power is not stated in the text; the Court explained it in 1803. Judges are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and serve during good behavior.
rows.us_zh: 一般的聯邦法院，最上面是最高法院。這項權力條文沒有明寫，最高法院在 1803 年說明了它的道理。法官由總統提名、參議院同意，品行端正即終身任職。
rows.tw_en: The Judicial Yuan interprets the Constitution (Article 78). The Additional Articles provide for fifteen justices, nominated by the President and confirmed by the Legislative Yuan for terms of eight years, who also sit as the Constitutional Court (Additional Article 5).
rows.tw_zh: 司法院解釋憲法（憲法第 78 條）。增修條文規定司法院設大法官十五人，由總統提名、經立法院同意任命，任期八年，並組成憲法法庭（增修條文第 5 條）。

quotes.cite_zh: 中華民國憲法增修條文　第 3 條第 2 項第 2 款（覆議）
quotes.cite_en: Additional Articles of the Constitution, Article 3, Paragraph 2, Item 2 (reconsideration)
quotes.text: 行政院對於立法院決議之法律案、預算案、條約案，如認為有窒礙難行時，得經總統之核可，於該決議案送達行政院十日內，移請立法院覆議。立法院對於行政院移請覆議案，應於送達十五日內作成決議。如為休會期間，立法院應於七日內自行集會，並於開議十五日內作成決議。覆議案逾期未議決者，原決議失效。覆議時，如經全體立法委員二分之一以上決議維持原案，行政院院長應即接受該決議。
quotes.en: Official English translation: “Should the Executive Yuan deem a statutory, budgetary, or treaty bill passed by the Legislative Yuan difficult to execute, the Executive Yuan may, with the approval of the president of the Republic and within ten days of the bill's submission to the Executive Yuan, request the Legislative Yuan to reconsider the bill. The Legislative Yuan shall reach a resolution on the returned bill within 15 days after it is received. Should the Legislative Yuan be in recess, it shall convene of its own accord within seven days and reach a resolution within 15 days after the session begins. Should the Legislative Yuan not reach a resolution within the said period of time, the original bill shall become invalid. Should more than one-half of the total number of Legislative Yuan members uphold the original bill, the president of the Executive Yuan shall immediately accept the said bill.”

quotes.cite_zh: 中華民國憲法增修條文　第 3 條第 2 項第 3 款（不信任案）
quotes.cite_en: Additional Articles of the Constitution, Article 3, Paragraph 2, Item 3 (vote of no confidence)
quotes.text: 立法院得經全體立法委員三分之一以上連署，對行政院院長提出不信任案。不信任案提出七十二小時後，應於四十八小時內以記名投票表決之。如經全體立法委員二分之一以上贊成，行政院院長應於十日內提出辭職，並得同時呈請總統解散立法院；不信任案如未獲通過，一年內不得對同一行政院院長再提不信任案。
quotes.en: Official English translation: “With the signatures of more than one-third of the total number of Legislative Yuan members, the Legislative Yuan may propose a no-confidence vote against the president of the Executive Yuan. Seventy-two hours after the no-confidence motion is made, an open-ballot vote shall be taken within 48 hours. Should more than one-half of the total number of Legislative Yuan members approve the motion, the president of the Executive Yuan shall tender his resignation within ten days, and at the same time may request that the president dissolve the Legislative Yuan. Should the no-confidence motion fail, the Legislative Yuan may not initiate another no-confidence motion against the same president of the Executive Yuan within one year.”

taiwan.note_en: Two things to notice. First, the numbers differ: a returned bill needs two thirds of each of two houses in the United States and more than half of all members of the Legislative Yuan, which has one chamber, in Taiwan. Second, the default differs: an American bill left alone for ten days becomes law, while a request for reconsideration that is not decided in time causes the original bill to lapse. The text was checked against the Laws and Regulations Database in October 2026.
taiwan.note_zh: 有兩點可以注意。第一，數字不同：被退回的法案，在美國要兩院各三分之二才能維持，在台灣是全體立法委員二分之一以上（立法院只有一院）。第二，「沒有動作時」的結果不同：美國的法案放著十天不處理就成為法律；台灣的覆議案逾期沒有議決，原決議就失效。條文於 2026 年 10 月對過全國法規資料庫。

news_english.en: Eight terms for reading about the three branches
news_english.zh: 讀三權新聞用得到的八個詞
news_english.lead_en: Listen to each term and its example sentence, then try making a sentence of your own. Most of the examples come from history.
news_english.lead_zh: 先聽每個詞和例句，再試著自己造一句。例句大多取自歷史。

items.def_en: the powers that let each branch limit the others
items.def_zh: 讓每個部門都能限制其他部門的那些權力
items.ex: The veto is part of the system of checks and balances.
items.ex_zh: 否決是制衡制度的一部分。

items.def_en: (of a president) to refuse to sign a bill and send it back to Congress
items.def_zh: （總統）拒絕簽署法案並退回國會
items.ex: George Washington was the first president to veto a bill, in 1792.
items.ex_zh: 華盛頓在 1792 年成為第一位否決法案的總統。

items.def_en: (of Congress) to pass a vetoed bill again by two thirds of each house
items.def_zh: （國會）以兩院各三分之二再次通過被否決的法案
items.ex: Congress did not manage to override a veto until 1845.
items.ex_zh: 國會直到 1845 年才第一次成功推翻否決。

items.def_en: (of the Senate) to approve a person the president has nominated
items.def_zh: （參議院）同意總統提名的人選
items.ex: In 1795 the Senate refused to confirm a nominee for chief justice.
items.ex_zh: 1795 年，參議院拒絕同意一位首席大法官的提名人選。

items.def_en: (of the House) to bring formal charges against an official; it is not the same as removing the official
items.def_zh: （眾議院）對官員正式提出指控；彈劾不等於免職
items.ex: The House voted to impeach President Andrew Johnson in 1868, but the Senate did not convict him.
items.ex_zh: 1868 年眾議院表決彈劾安德魯．詹森總統，但參議院沒有將他定罪。

items.def_en: the power of courts to decide whether a law or an official act agrees with the Constitution
items.def_zh: 法院判斷法律或官方作為是否合乎憲法的權力
items.ex: The reasoning behind judicial review was set out in Marbury v. Madison.
items.ex_zh: 司法審查背後的道理，是在 Marbury v. Madison 案裡說明的。

items.def_en: Congress's control over what the government may spend
items.def_zh: 國會對政府可以花多少錢的控制權
items.ex: Under Article I, Congress holds the power of the purse.
items.ex_zh: 依第一條，錢包的權力在國會手上。

items.def_en: a situation in which the branches cannot agree and nothing gets passed
items.def_zh: 各部門無法達成一致、什麼都通不過的狀況
items.ex: Critics of divided power say that it leads to gridlock.
items.ex_zh: 批評權力分散的人說，這種制度會造成僵局。

myths.myth_en: Separation of powers means that each branch works alone in its own area.
myths.myth_zh: 權力分立的意思是：每個部門各管各的，互不相干。
myths.fact_en: The branches are separate in their membership, but their powers overlap on purpose. The President takes part in lawmaking, the Senate in appointments, and the courts in judging what the other two have done. Madison's phrase for this was “partial agency.”
myths.fact_zh: 三個部門的成員是分開的，權力卻刻意重疊：總統參與立法，參議院參與人事任命，法院則審查另外兩個部門做的事。麥迪遜把這叫做「部分的參與」。

myths.myth_en: To impeach an official is to remove that official from office.
myths.myth_zh: 彈劾一名官員，就是把他免職。
myths.fact_en: Impeachment is only the accusation, made by the House. Removal requires a trial in the Senate and a conviction by two thirds of the members present. As of 2026 the House has impeached officials twenty-two times, and eight have been convicted.
myths.fact_zh: 彈劾只是指控，由眾議院提出。要免職，還得經過參議院審判，並由出席議員三分之二定罪。到 2026 年為止，眾議院彈劾過二十二次，被定罪的有八人。

myths.myth_en: The Constitution says that the Supreme Court may strike down laws.
myths.myth_zh: 憲法明文規定最高法院可以宣告法律無效。
myths.fact_en: It does not say so in words. The Supreme Court's own account is that “the function of judicial review is not explicitly provided in the Constitution,” though “it had been anticipated before the adoption of that document.” The Court set out the reasoning in Marbury v. Madison in 1803.
myths.fact_zh: 條文裡沒有這樣的字句。最高法院自己的說明是：司法審查這項功能「在憲法中並無明文規定」，不過「在憲法通過之前就已經有人預期到它」。這項權力的道理，是最高法院在 1803 年的 Marbury v. Madison 案裡說明的。

myths.myth_en: A veto kills a bill, and a bill cannot become law without the President's signature.
myths.myth_zh: 否決就是法案的終點；沒有總統簽署，法案不可能成為法律。
myths.fact_en: There are two ways around the signature. Congress can override a veto by two thirds of each house, and a bill that the President neither signs nor returns within ten days becomes law if Congress is still in session. Only the pocket veto cannot be overridden.
myths.fact_zh: 繞過簽署的路有兩條：國會可以用兩院各三分之二推翻否決；總統在十天內既不簽署也不退回的法案，只要國會還在開會，就自動成為法律。只有口袋否決是國會無法推翻的。

activities.title_en: Find the Checks in the Text

materials.en: Articles I, II, and III of the Constitution, from the National Archives transcription (linked in the sources below)
materials.zh: 憲法第一、二、三條（國家檔案館的謄本，連結在下面的出處裡）

materials.en: A sheet of paper with a large triangle drawn on it, the corners labeled Congress, President, and Courts
materials.zh: 一張紙，上面畫一個大三角形，三個角分別寫上國會、總統、法院

materials.en: Three colored pens, one for each branch
materials.zh: 三枝不同顏色的筆，一個部門一種顏色

steps.en: Skim the three articles and mark every sentence in which one branch takes part in, approves, or can undo the work of another. Aim for at least six.
steps.zh: 瀏覽這三條，把「一個部門參與、同意，或者可以推翻另一個部門的工作」的句子都標出來。目標是至少找到六句。

steps.en: For each sentence, draw an arrow on the triangle from the branch that acts to the branch it checks, in the color of the acting branch, and write the article and section beside it.
steps.zh: 每一句都在三角形上畫一道箭頭，從出手的部門指向被牽制的部門，用出手那個部門的顏色，並在旁邊寫上是第幾條第幾項。

steps.en: Count the arrows leaving each corner. Which branch has the most ways to check the others? Which has the fewest?
steps.zh: 數一數從每個角出發的箭頭。哪個部門牽制別人的辦法最多？哪個最少？

steps.en: Compare your triangle with the grid in the 3D model. Is there a direction for which you found no clause? Explain why that might be.
steps.zh: 把你的三角形和 3D 模型裡的方格比一比。有沒有哪個方向你找不到條文？說說可能的原因。

activities.tip_en: Many readers find no clause that plainly says a court may set a law aside; the nearest is Article III, Section 2, which extends the judicial power to cases “arising under this Constitution.” That is the point of the third myth card above.
activities.tip_zh: 很多人會發現：找不到哪一條明白寫著法院可以宣告法律無效；最接近的是第三條第二項，它讓司法權及於「因本憲法而生」的案件。這正是上面第三張迷思卡要說的。

materials.en: The “After the Veto, What Then?” tool above
materials.zh: 上面的「否決之後，還有幾條路？」小工具

materials.en: Paper for a table with four columns: House votes, Senate votes, the President's choice, and the result

lessons.title: Why Does Every State Have Its Own Laws?
lessons.title_zh: 為什麼每一州的法律不一樣？
lessons.level: 高中以上 · High school and up
lessons.blurb_en: Choose a power, such as coining money, running schools, or collecting taxes, and see which layer of a 3D map lights up: the national government, the states, or both. Then compare all fifty states on one question at a time, read Federalist No. 45 and McCulloch v. Maryland, and weigh local choice against national standards.
lessons.blurb_zh: 選一項權力——鑄幣、辦學校、徵稅——看 3D 地圖上亮起來的是哪一層：全國政府、各州，還是兩層都亮。接著一次一個題目比較五十州，讀《聯邦論》第四十五篇與 McCulloch v. Maryland，再想想該由地方決定，還是該有全國一致的標準。
lessons.big_idea_en: Federalism divides power between two levels of government. Some powers belong to the national government, some remain with the states, and some are shared. That is why one question can have fifty different answers across the country, and why, when the two levels collide, the Constitution's Supremacy Clause decides which law prevails.
lessons.big_idea_zh: 聯邦制把權力分給兩層政府：有些權力屬於全國政府，有些留給各州，有些兩邊共有。所以同一個問題，在全國可以有五十種不同的答案；而兩層衝突時，由憲法的最高條款決定哪一邊的法律優先。

powers.en: Coining money
powers.zh: 鑄造貨幣
powers.text_en: Only the national government issues money. The Constitution gives the power to Congress and, in a separate clause, forbids the states to coin money. That is why a dollar is the same in every state.
powers.text_zh: 只有全國政府發行貨幣。憲法把這項權力交給國會，又在另一條明文禁止各州鑄幣。所以一塊錢在每一州都一樣。
powers.quote: No State shall enter into any Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation; grant Letters of Marque and Reprisal; coin Money; …

powers.en: Declaring war and raising armies
powers.zh: 宣戰與建軍
powers.text_en: Defense belongs to the national government. Congress declares war and raises the army and navy, and the states may not keep troops or ships of war in peacetime without Congress's consent.
powers.text_zh: 國防屬於全國政府。宣戰、招募陸海軍都由國會負責；平時各州未經國會同意，不得維持軍隊或戰艦。
powers.quote: To declare War, grant Letters of Marque and Reprisal, and make Rules concerning Captures on Land and Water;

powers.en: Making treaties
powers.zh: 締結條約
powers.text_en: The President makes treaties with the consent of two thirds of the senators present. The states are forbidden to enter into “any Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation.”
powers.text_zh: 總統經出席參議員三分之二同意締結條約；各州則被禁止締結「任何條約、同盟或邦聯」。
powers.quote: No State shall enter into any Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation; …

powers.en: Setting the rules for becoming a citizen
powers.zh: 訂定入籍的規則
powers.text_en: The rules for becoming a citizen are national and the same everywhere. A person naturalized in one state is a citizen of the United States and of whatever state he or she lives in.
powers.text_zh: 入籍的規則是全國性的，各地都一樣。在任何一州歸化的人，都是美國公民，也是他所居住那一州的公民。
powers.quote: To establish an uniform Rule of Naturalization, …

powers.en: Post offices and post roads
powers.zh: 郵局與郵路
powers.text_en: The Constitution gives Congress the power to establish post offices. A letter mailed in one state carries the same national stamp in every other.
powers.text_zh: 憲法把設立郵局的權力交給國會。在任何一州寄出的信，貼的都是同一種全國通用的郵票。
powers.quote: To establish Post Offices and post Roads;

powers.en: Running public schools
powers.zh: 辦公立學校
powers.text_en: Education is not among the powers the Constitution gives the national government, so it falls under the powers “reserved to the States.” States, and the school districts they create, set graduation requirements and run the schools.
powers.text_zh: 教育不在憲法交給全國政府的權力之列，所以屬於「保留給各州」的權力。畢業的條件由各州——以及各州設立的學區——決定，學校也由他們辦。
powers.quote: The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.

powers.en: Licenses for driving and for marriage
powers.zh: 駕照與結婚登記
powers.text_en: Driver's licenses are issued by each state's motor vehicle agency, and marriage licenses by the states as well, under state law. That is why the requirements and the paperwork are not the same everywhere.
powers.text_zh: 駕照由各州的監理機關核發，結婚證書也由各州依州法核發。所以各地的條件與手續並不相同。
powers.cite: Reserved powers (Tenth Amendment) · 保留給各州的權力（第十條修正案）

powers.en: Defining most crimes
powers.zh: 規定大部分的罪行
powers.text_en: Most criminal cases, like most family-law cases, are heard in state courts under state law. Federal criminal law covers matters tied to the national government's powers, such as counterfeiting money.
powers.text_zh: 大部分的刑事案件——和大部分的家事案件一樣——是在州法院依州法審理的。聯邦刑法管的是和全國政府權力有關的事，例如偽造貨幣。
powers.cite: Reserved powers (Tenth Amendment) · 保留給各州的權力（第十條修正案）

powers.en: Collecting taxes
powers.zh: 徵稅
powers.text_en: Both levels tax the same people at the same time. Congress may “lay and collect Taxes,” and the states keep their own power to tax, apart from a few limits, such as the rule that a state may not tax imports or exports without Congress's consent.
powers.text_zh: 兩層政府同時向同一批人課稅。國會可以「課徵各種稅捐」，各州也保有自己的徵稅權，只受少數限制——例如未經國會同意，州不得對進出口貨物課稅。
powers.quote: The Congress shall have Power To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, …

powers.en: Running courts
powers.zh: 設立法院
powers.text_en: There are two court systems side by side: federal courts under Article III, and the courts of each state under its own constitution. State courts hear most criminal, contract, and family-law cases. Lesson 14 follows a case up both ladders.
powers.text_zh: 有兩套法院並排存在：依第三條設立的聯邦法院，以及各州依自己的憲法設立的法院。大部分的刑事、契約與家事案件由州法院審理。第十四課會跟著一個案子，沿著兩道階梯往上走。
powers.quote: The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.

powers.en: Running elections for Congress
powers.zh: 辦國會議員選舉
powers.text_en: The states set the times, places, and manner of elections for Congress, and Congress may change those rules by law. In practice, the states organize the voting.
powers.text_zh: 國會議員選舉的時間、地點與方式由各州規定，國會則可以用法律加以修改。實際上，投票是由各州在辦理。
powers.quote: The Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and Representatives, shall be prescribed in each State by the Legislature thereof; but the Congress may at any time by Law make or alter such Regulations, …

src.label: Nebraska Legislature: Facts about the Unicameral

paras: An American lives under two governments at the same time. One is the national government in Washington, usually called the federal government. The other is the government of the state where the person lives, with its own constitution, legislature, governor, and courts. Dividing power between two levels in this way is called federalism. It explains why the rate of sales tax, the requirements for a driver's license, and the punishment for many crimes change at a state line, while the dollar in a wallet, the stamp on a letter, and the rules for becoming a citizen are the same everywhere. In Madison's words, the two levels are “different agents and trustees of the people.”

State governments came first. When the Constitution was written, the thirteen states already had governments of their own, and few Americans wanted to see them swallowed by a distant capital. The Constitution therefore gave the national government a list of specific powers and left the rest where it was. James Madison put it plainly in The Federalist No. 45. The powers given to the national government, he wrote, “are few and defined,” while those that remain with the states “are numerous and indefinite.” The national government would deal mainly with matters such as war, peace, and foreign commerce, and the states with the ordinary affairs of daily life.

Powers under the Constitution fall into a few groups. Enumerated powers are the ones listed for Congress, such as coining money, declaring war, and running the post office. Reserved powers are the ones left to the states by the Tenth Amendment, which says that powers not delegated to the United States “are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.” Education, family law, and most criminal law belong here. Concurrent powers, such as taxing, borrowing, and running courts, are held by both levels at once. Finally, some powers are denied to the states outright. No state may coin money or make a treaty, and no state may tax imports without the consent of Congress.

The boundary between the levels has never stayed still. In 1818 Maryland passed a law taxing a branch of the Bank of the United States, which Congress had created even though the Constitution says nothing about banks; the dispute reached the Supreme Court in 1819. In McCulloch v. Maryland, Chief Justice John Marshall upheld the bank under the clause that lets Congress make all laws “necessary and proper” for carrying out its listed powers, and he held that a state could not tax it, since “the power to tax involves the power to destroy.” Maryland had argued for reading the national government's powers narrowly. The Court read them to include the means of carrying them out, and held that a state may not obstruct a valid federal law.

Two other tools have widened the national government's reach. The first is the Commerce Clause, which lets Congress regulate commerce “among the several States.” In Gibbons v. Ogden in 1824, the Supreme Court held that commerce includes navigation, so that steamboats licensed by Congress could not be shut out by a monopoly that New York had granted. Over time Congress has relied on that clause for a growing share of national laws, and how far it reaches is still argued. The second tool is money. Congress can attach conditions to the funds it sends the states. In 1984 Congress passed a law that withheld part of a state's federal highway funds unless it made twenty-one the minimum age for buying alcohol, and by 1988 every state had done so.

Federalism has been used for good and ill. Before the Civil War, claims of “states' rights” were used to defend slavery, and later to defend racial segregation. Yet national power was also turned to slavery's ends: the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required the return of people who had escaped, and some Northern states passed laws to resist it. After the war, the Fourteenth Amendment forbade any state to deny a person “the equal protection of the laws.” In 1957, when the governor of Arkansas used the state's National Guard to keep Black students out of Central High School in Little Rock, President Eisenhower sent federal troops to enforce desegregation.

The same division also lets states try ideas that the nation has not adopted. Justice Louis Brandeis wrote in 1932 that “a single courageous state may, if its citizens choose, serve as a laboratory; and try novel social and economic experiments without risk to the rest of the country.” History offers examples. Nine western states had adopted woman suffrage by 1912, years before the Nineteenth Amendment secured the vote for women across the country in 1920. Nebraska has run its legislature with a single chamber since 1937, while every other state has two. An idea that works in one state can be copied by others, and one that fails stays contained.

The result is a country in which the answer to many questions depends on where you live. That variety is one of the purposes of the system, and it is also one of its costs. People who move from one state to another must learn new rules, businesses must follow fifty sets of laws, and a right may seem broader in one state than in the next. Americans have argued since 1787 about which matters should be settled close to home and which deserve one national standard, and the line has moved many times. The map in this lesson shows what that division looks like on a handful of questions that are not matters of party dispute.
paras_zh: 一個美國人同時生活在兩個政府之下。一個是在華盛頓的全國政府，通常叫做聯邦政府（federal government）；另一個是他居住那一州的政府，有自己的憲法、議會、州長和法院。像這樣把權力分給兩層政府，叫做聯邦制（federalism）。它說明了為什麼銷售稅的稅率、考駕照的條件、許多罪行的刑罰，一跨過州界就不一樣；而皮夾裡的一塊錢、信封上的郵票、入籍的規則，卻到處都相同。用麥迪遜的話說，兩層政府是「人民不同的代理人與受託人」。
州政府比聯邦政府先存在。寫憲法的時候，十三個州早已有了自己的政府，很少美國人願意看到它們被一個遙遠的首都吞掉。因此，憲法給全國政府一張列明的權力清單，其餘的權力則留在原處。麥迪遜在《聯邦論》第四十五篇講得很清楚：交給全國政府的權力「少而明確」，留給各州的則「多而不定」。全國政府主要處理戰爭、和平、對外貿易這一類的事，各州處理的是日常生活的一般事務。

憲法之下的權力可以分成幾類。列舉的權力（enumerated powers）是明列給國會的，例如鑄幣、宣戰、經營郵政。保留的權力（reserved powers）是第十條修正案留給各州的——條文說，沒有授予合眾國的權力，「保留給各州，或保留給人民」；教育、家庭法和大部分的刑法屬於這一類。共有的權力（concurrent powers），例如徵稅、舉債、設立法院，則由兩層政府同時擁有。最後，有些權力是明文禁止各州行使的：任何一州都不得鑄幣、不得締結條約；未經國會同意，也不得對進口貨物課稅。

兩層之間的界線從來沒有停在原地。1818 年，馬里蘭州通過法律，對美國銀行設在當地的分行課稅——這家銀行是國會設立的，雖然憲法對銀行一個字也沒提；這場爭議在 1819 年打到最高法院。在 McCulloch v. Maryland 案中，首席大法官馬歇爾援引容許國會制定一切「必要且適當」法律以執行其列舉權力的條款，判定這家銀行合憲；他也判定州不得對它課稅，因為「課稅的權力包含毀滅的權力」。馬里蘭主張對全國政府的權力作狹義的解讀；最高法院則把這些權力解讀為包括執行它們的手段，並判定州不得阻撓有效的聯邦法律。

另外有兩項工具擴大了全國政府的範圍。第一項是商業條款（Commerce Clause），讓國會管理「各州之間的貿易」。1824 年的 Gibbons v. Ogden 案，最高法院判定「貿易」包括航運，所以領有國會執照的汽船，不能被紐約州授予的獨占權擋在門外。隨著時間過去，國會越來越常援引這項條款來制定全國性的法律，而它能延伸到多遠，至今仍有爭論。第二項工具是錢：國會可以在撥給各州的款項上附加條件。1984 年，國會通過一項法律：州若不把購買酒類的最低年齡訂為二十一歲，就扣下它一部分的聯邦公路經費；到 1988 年，每一州都照做了。

聯邦制被用來做過好事，也做過壞事。內戰之前，「州權」（states' rights）的主張被用來為奴隸制辯護，後來又被用來為種族隔離辯護。可是全國政府的權力也曾被用來替奴隸制服務：1850 年的《逃亡奴隸法》要求交還逃走的人，而北方有些州通過法律加以抵制。內戰之後，第十四條修正案禁止任何一州拒絕給予任何人「法律的平等保護」。1957 年，阿肯色州州長動用州的國民警衛隊（National Guard），阻止黑人學生進入小岩城的中央中學；艾森豪總統派出聯邦部隊，強制執行廢除種族隔離。

同樣的分權，也讓各州可以嘗試全國還沒採用的做法。布蘭戴斯大法官在 1932 年寫道：「一個勇敢的州，只要它的公民願意，就可以充當一間實驗室，嘗試新的社會與經濟實驗，而不會危及國家的其他部分。」歷史上有例子：到 1912 年，西部已經有九個州通過了婦女投票權，比 1920 年第十九條修正案替全國的女性確保投票權早了好幾年。內布拉斯加從 1937 年起，州議會只有一院，其他每一州都是兩院。一州行得通的做法，別州可以照著學；行不通的，也只限於那一州。
結果是：一個國家裡，很多問題的答案取決於你住在哪裡。這種多樣性是這套制度的用意之一，也是它的代價之一。從一州搬到另一州的人得重新學一套規則，企業得遵守五十套法律，同一種權利在這一州和鄰州看起來也可能寬窄不同。從 1787 年起，美國人就一直在爭論哪些事該在離家近的地方決定、哪些事該有全國一致的標準，這條線也移動過很多次。這一課的地圖，用幾個不屬於政黨爭議的題目，讓你看看這種分權是什麼樣子。
questions: Explain the difference between enumerated, reserved, and concurrent powers, and give one example of each.
In McCulloch v. Maryland, what two questions did the Court answer, and why does each matter for the balance between the national government and the states?

The reading says that federalism “has been used for good and ill.” Use two examples from the reading, one for each, and explain what they suggest about whether either level of government is automatically the protector of rights.
answers: Enumerated powers are the ones the Constitution lists for Congress, such as coining money. Reserved powers are left to the states by the Tenth Amendment, such as running public schools. Concurrent powers belong to both levels at the same time, such as collecting taxes.

First, could Congress create a bank when the Constitution does not mention one? Yes, because the Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress choose the means of carrying out its listed powers. This allowed national power to grow beyond the bare list. Second, could Maryland tax the bank? No, because a state may not obstruct a valid federal law, and “the power to tax involves the power to destroy.” This confirmed that valid federal law is supreme over state law.

Sample answer: “States' rights” arguments were used to defend slavery and segregation, but the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 used national power on slavery's side, while some Northern states resisted it. In 1957 federal troops enforced desegregation against a state governor. The examples suggest that neither level is automatically the protector of rights; it depends on what each level does with its power.

quiz.q: A state wants to issue its own coins to celebrate its anniversary as legal money. Why can't it?
options: The Tenth Amendment forbids states from celebrating anniversaries
Article I, Section 10 says no state shall coin money
Only cities may issue money
The governor would need the Supreme Court's permission

quiz.q: The Constitution says nothing about public schools. Under the Tenth Amendment, what follows?
options: Public schools are unconstitutional
Congress must run all public schools
Running schools is a power reserved to the states or to the people
Each school must ask the President for approval

options: To argue that states should abolish all taxes
To explain why a state could not tax an institution created by Congress, since a tax could be used to drive it out
To show that Congress has no power to tax
To praise Maryland's tax system

options: It amended the Constitution, which shows how easy amendments are
It sued every state, which shows the power of the courts

Federalism ended with the Civil War
Power at either level has been used both to protect rights and to deny them

questions.en: Printing and coining money
questions.zh: 印製與鑄造貨幣
questions.why_en: Congress has the power “To coin Money,” and Article I, Section 10 forbids the states to do so.
questions.why_zh: 國會有「鑄造貨幣」的權力，第一條第十項則禁止各州鑄幣。
questions.hint_en: Is a dollar different in each state?
questions.hint_zh: 一塊錢在每一州都不一樣嗎？

questions.en: Setting the requirements for a high school diploma
questions.zh: 訂定高中畢業的條件
questions.why_en: Education is a reserved power. States and the school districts they create decide what students must complete.
questions.why_zh: 教育是保留給各州的權力。學生要修完什麼，由各州和各州設立的學區決定。
questions.hint_en: Is education on the list of Congress's powers?
questions.hint_zh: 教育在國會的權力清單上嗎？

questions.en: Collecting taxes on income
questions.zh: 課徵所得稅
questions.why_en: Congress taxes incomes (the Sixteenth Amendment), and the states keep their own power to tax, which can include taxing incomes.
questions.why_zh: 國會課徵所得稅（第十六條修正案），各州也保有自己的徵稅權，可以包括對所得課稅。
questions.hint_en: Can two governments tax the same paycheck?
questions.hint_zh: 兩個政府可以對同一份薪水課稅嗎？

questions.en: Declaring war
questions.zh: 宣戰
questions.why_en: Congress declares war, and the states may not engage in war unless actually invaded.
questions.why_zh: 宣戰由國會決定；各州除非真的遭到入侵，否則不得參與戰爭。
questions.hint_en: Could one state be at war while another is at peace?
questions.hint_zh: 有可能一州在打仗、另一州在和平嗎？

questions.en: Issuing a driver's license
questions.zh: 核發駕照
questions.why_en: Licenses are issued by each state's motor vehicle agency under state law, so the requirements differ from state to state.
questions.why_zh: 駕照由各州的監理機關依州法核發，所以各州的條件不同。
questions.hint_en: Which office do you visit to take the test?
questions.hint_zh: 考駕照要去哪裡的機關？

questions.en: Running a system of courts
questions.zh: 設立法院體系
questions.why_en: Federal courts exist under Article III, and every state has its own courts; most cases are heard in state courts.
questions.why_zh: 聯邦法院依第三條設立，每一州也有自己的法院；大部分的案件在州法院審理。
questions.hint_en: Where is a traffic ticket contested, and where is a case about a federal law?
questions.hint_zh: 交通罰單在哪裡爭執？關於聯邦法律的案子又在哪裡審？

questions.en: Setting the rules for becoming a citizen
questions.zh: 訂定入籍的規則
questions.why_en: Congress has the power to establish “an uniform Rule of Naturalization.”
questions.why_zh: 國會有權訂定「全國一致的歸化規則」。
questions.hint_en: Look for the word “uniform” in Article I, Section 8.
questions.hint_zh: 到第一條第八項找 uniform 這個字。

questions.en: Issuing marriage licenses
questions.zh: 核發結婚證書
questions.why_en: Marriage licenses are issued by the states, and family law, including marriage, is mainly state law heard in state courts.
questions.why_zh: 結婚證書由各州核發；家庭法（包括婚姻）主要是州法，由州法院審理。
questions.hint_en: This is part of family law.
questions.hint_zh: 這屬於家庭法。

questions.en: Borrowing money
questions.zh: 舉債
questions.why_en: Congress may borrow “on the credit of the United States,” and states borrow too, for example by selling bonds for roads and schools.
questions.why_zh: 國會可以「以合眾國的信用」舉債，各州也會借錢，例如發行公債來修路、蓋學校。
questions.hint_en: Do both levels build things they cannot pay for at once?
questions.hint_zh: 兩層政府是不是都會蓋一時付不起的東西？

questions.en: Making a treaty with another country
questions.zh: 與外國締結條約
questions.why_en: The President makes treaties with the Senate's consent, and Article I, Section 10 forbids the states to enter into any treaty.
questions.why_zh: 總統經參議院同意締結條約，第一條第十項則禁止各州締結任何條約。
questions.hint_en: Article I, Section 10 begins with this.
questions.hint_zh: 第一條第十項一開頭就寫了這件事。

match.end_en: Notice that “both” is not a rare answer. Much of what governments do is shared, and that is where the Supremacy Clause matters most.

items.text: The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.
items.zh: 本憲法未授予合眾國、也未禁止各州行使的權力，分別保留給各州，或保留給人民。

items.cite_en: Article I, Section 8, Clauses 3 and 18 (commerce; necessary and proper)

items.text: To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes; … To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers, and all other Powers vested by this Constitution in the Government of the United States, or in any Department or Officer thereof.
items.zh: 管理與外國、各州之間以及與印第安部族的貿易；……制定為執行上述各項權力，以及本憲法授予合眾國政府或其任何部門、官員的一切其他權力所必要且適當的一切法律。
items.note_en: These two clauses, read together, are the main source of the national government's growth. The word “Commerce” and the phrase “necessary and proper” do not say how far they reach, and that question has been argued in court since McCulloch v. Maryland in 1819.
items.note_zh: 這兩款合在一起讀，是全國政府擴大的主要來源。「貿易」這個字和「必要且適當」這個片語都沒有說它們能延伸多遠；從 1819 年的 McCulloch v. Maryland 案起，這個問題就一直在法院裡爭論。

items.cite_en: Article I, Section 10, Clause 1 (limits on the states)

items.text: No State shall enter into any Treaty, Alliance, or Confederation; grant Letters of Marque and Reprisal; coin Money; emit Bills of Credit; make any Thing but gold and silver Coin a Tender in Payment of Debts; pass any Bill of Attainder, ex post facto Law, or Law impairing the Obligation of Contracts, or grant any Title of Nobility.
items.zh: 任何一州都不得締結條約、同盟或邦聯；不得頒發捕獲敵船許可狀；不得鑄造貨幣；不得發行信用票據；不得以金銀幣以外的任何物品作為償還債務的法定貨幣；不得通過褫奪公權法案、溯及既往的法律或損害契約義務的法律；也不得授予任何貴族爵位。
items.note_en: The Constitution also limits what the states may do, not only what the national government may do. Several of these limits ended practices that had caused trouble under the Articles of Confederation, when states issued their own money.
items.note_zh: 憲法不只限制全國政府能做什麼，也限制各州。其中幾項限制，終結了《邦聯條例》時期各州自己發行貨幣所造成的麻煩。

primary.zh: 麥迪遜的承諾，馬歇爾的解讀
primary.lead_en: Two texts thirty-one years apart. In 1788 Madison assured readers that the new national government would have only a few powers. In 1819 Marshall explained how far those powers reach. Read each slowly before you open the translation; the spelling and punctuation are those of the sources.
primary.lead_zh: 兩段相隔三十一年的文字。1788 年，麥迪遜向讀者保證新的全國政府只會有少數幾項權力；1819 年，馬歇爾說明這些權力能延伸多遠。先慢慢讀一遍，再打開中譯；拼法與標點照出處原樣。

docs.by_en: By James Madison, signed “Publius.” Printed in a New York newspaper in late January 1788; the editors of Madison's papers date it January 26.
docs.by_zh: 麥迪遜著，署名「普布利烏斯」（Publius）。1788 年 1 月底刊登於紐約的一份報紙；《麥迪遜文集》的編者把日期定在 1 月 26 日。
text: The powers delegated by the proposed constitution to the federal government, are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the state governments are numerous and indefinite. The former will be exercised principally on external objects, as war, peace, negociation, and foreign commerce; with which last the power of taxation will for the most part be connected. The powers reserved to the several states will extend to all the objects, which, in the ordinary course of affairs, concern the lives, liberties and properties of the people; and the internal order, improvement and prosperity of the state.
text_zh: 擬議中的憲法授予聯邦政府的權力，少而明確；仍留在各州政府的權力，多而不定。前者主要行使於對外的事務，如戰爭、和平、談判與對外貿易；徵稅的權力大多和最後這一項相連。保留給各州的權力，則涵蓋日常事務中一切關係到人民的生命、自由與財產，以及各州內部的秩序、改善與繁榮的事項。
docs.note_en: Text as given by Founders Online (National Archives), from The Papers of James Madison, which keeps the spelling “negociation.” The Library of Congress text punctuates the passage differently, capitalizes “Constitution” and “State,” and dates the essay January 25. Public domain. The Chinese translation is ours.
docs.note_zh: 原文依 Founders Online（美國國家檔案館）收錄的《麥迪遜文集》，保留 negociation 的舊拼法。國會圖書館的文本標點不同、Constitution 與 State 用大寫，日期標為 1 月 25 日。公有領域。中譯為本站所譯。
